abstract: The conservation of African savanna ecosystems is recognized as making important contributions toward capturing and storing atmospheric carbon in vegetation and in soils to help mitigate climate change. Also, savannas are important for elephant conservation, which is an increasing priority throughout Africa. However, there is concern that elephants can damage and transform vegetation thereby compromising savanna ecosystems capacities to capture and store carbon. Yet, elephants can have positive effects by releasing body wastes that contribute to nutrient cycling to enhance vegetation productivity (and hence carbon capture). The release of carbon in dung and trampling of soils can enhance long-term carbon storage in soils. Thus, an ecologically holistic assessment of net elephant effects on carbon capture and storage requires accounting for the negative and positive effects together. We report on a holistic assessment of elephant effects using a carbon cycle model that compares savanna ecosystem carbon capture and storage between scenarios with and without elephants. The modeling estimates that elephants at a density of approximately 0.5 individuals per square kilometer could increase average net ecosystem carbon capture by 1.4 times (range of uncertainty of 0.4 to 5.5 times). Elephants are estimated to increase average long-term aboveground carbon stocks by 6.5 times (uncertainty of 2 to 10 times). Average long-term soil carbon storage is estimated to increase by 1.7 times (uncertainty of 0.6 to 5.3 times). The estimated annual carbon capture is large enough to be considered a negative emission in national emissions accounting from land use change, suggesting that savanna elephant conservation should be considered as a nature-based climate solution.
